newsitem.title: UK: Container deal shifts heavy P&O burden.
newsitem.headline: Container deal shifts heavy P&O burden.

text.p: One of the biggest liner shipping mergers of recent years, involving dozens of huge, modern container ships, will lift a heavy financial burden from the balance sheet of Britain's P&O, as well as its Dutch partner Nedlloyd NV.
The two companies said on Monday they would be putting their entire container shipping assets, including ships, boxes and most commercial operations, into a new jointly-owned company.
P&O, pooling the larger portion, will receive a one-off balancing payment of 113 million stg, and, once the assets have been moved, both firms expect the new unit to be self-financing.

Sources close to P&O said the cash payment would be "a significant" boost for its finances, which have long been a cause of concern among investors, and would also slice a big chunk off its balance sheet.

The value of the P&O assets being transferred into the combined P&O Nedlloyd was some 700 million stg at the end of December, 1995. Nedlloyd's container-related assets at the same stage were valued at about 500 million stg, the firms said.
Along with the assets, P&O Nedlloyd will also take over the debt financing of these from the two parents and will have inital total net borrowings of 300 million stg.
Beyond the capital change, with its potential short-term benefits, P&O and Nedlloyd assured shareholders in their statement that the deal could only improve profitability.

"Putting together the businesses...will enable far greater container volumes to be handled at much lower cost. This rationalisation has formed a key part of discussions between the parent companies over the past six months," they said.

Savings in excess of 129 million stg a year have already been identified from an annual cost base of 2.5 billion stg, the groups said, adding that "a substantial part of the savings is expected to be achieved before the end of 1997".
They see restructuring costs of about 65 million stg.

Compared with the high capital and carrying cost of many of their assets, the two component container lines have struggled for several years in an increasingly competitive and globalised market to make reasonable profits.

Despite high turnover and good utilisation rates, and a level of cash generation envied by many other industries, the two companies' net profits have been well below the level of returns achieved in many non-shipping businesses.
In 1995, they estimated, P&O container units made operating profits of 28 million stg, while Nedlloyd made 16 million.
The lines will combine to offer the world's biggest single fleet as measured by what P&O calls "standing slots".

But the relatively long haul nature of most of its routes will mean that P&O Nedlloyd will be smaller than both Taiwain's Evergreen and Denmark's Maersk Lines, owned by A.P. Moeller, in terms of loaded containers, a company source said.
In 1995 P&O had throughput of nearly 1.26 million teus (twenty foot equivalent units) and Nedlloyd 978,000.

Both lines operate a mixture of owned, leased and chartered ships with P&O at present running 52 vessels and Nedlloyd 60. Their combined fleet of containers will be 541,000 teu. -- Andrew Huddart, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8716
